[c] either cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical safeguards are implemented to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI during transmission.
whyItMatters: Unencrypted CUI on the wire or in the air can be read by anyone on the path.
evidenceExamples: Table listing every way CUI is transmitted (email, file share, VPN, Wi-Fi, web portal) and the encryption used for each
Screenshot of the email service's TLS enforcement or message-encryption settings (Microsoft Purview, Google S/MIME, Virtru, Preveil)
Screenshot of the VPN configuration showing the cipher suite (e.g., AES-256, IKEv2)
Screenshot of Wi-Fi settings showing WPA2/WPA3 (Enterprise preferred)
Screenshot of the SFTP/HTTPS file-transfer tool settings; evidence FTP/HTTP are disabled
Screenshot of the CMVP certificate for the module (ties to SC.L2-3.13.11)
aiReviewGuidance: Require the transmission-path table first; then expect a screenshot per path showing encryption. Email is the usual gap: opportunistic TLS alone is weak, so look for enforced TLS or message-level encryption for CUI. Reject if any listed path (e.g., Wi-Fi, file transfer) has no evidence, or if cleartext protocols are enabled. For Level 2, note whether the modules named are FIPS-validated. Assessors may test with configuration review or packet capture.
commonFailures: CUI emailed with no encryption beyond default TLS
FTP still used for customer file transfers
Guest or legacy Wi-Fi with WPA/WEP
Encryption present but not FIPS-validated

title: CUI Encryption
officialText: Employ FIPS-validated cryptography when used to protect the confidentiality of CUI.
plainEnglish: Wherever you rely on encryption to protect CUI (disk encryption, VPN, encrypted USB, email encryption), the encryption module must have a NIST FIPS 140 validation certificate, not just use a 'good algorithm'.
assessmentObjectives: [a] FIPS-validated cryptography is employed to protect the confidentiality of CUI.
whyItMatters: DoD only trusts encryption that has been independently tested; non-validated encryption counts as no encryption for CUI.
evidenceExamples: Table mapping each encryption use (BitLocker, FileVault, VPN, USB drives, email encryption, cloud storage) to its FIPS 140-2/140-3 certificate number
Screenshot of the NIST CMVP search result for each certificate number
Screenshot of Windows 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms' policy enabled, or the macOS FIPS module version
Screenshot of the firewall/VPN appliance in FIPS mode
Vendor documentation page stating the product's FIPS validation status (e.g., cloud provider FIPS endpoints)
aiReviewGuidance: Look for a mapping of every encryption use to a specific CMVP certificate number and a screenshot of that certificate's CMVP entry. 'Uses AES-256' is not evidence of validation; 'FIPS compliant' marketing language is not the same as validated. Reject if any encryption use from SC.L2-3.13.8, SC.L2-3.13.16, MP.L2-3.8.6, or MP.L2-3.8.9 has no certificate listed, or if certificates are listed as 'Historical' without an explanation. This is largely a documentation check and can be verified by the AI.
commonFailures: Consumer or open-source encryption tools with no FIPS validation
FIPS mode available but never enabled
Certificate numbers unknown; team assumes BitLocker is 'automatically FIPS'
Cloud services used via non-FIPS endpoints

title: Data at Rest
officialText: Protect the confidentiality of CUI at rest.
plainEnglish: CUI sitting on laptops, servers, phones, and cloud storage must be protected, normally by full-disk or file encryption, or by strong physical security where encryption is not practical.
assessmentObjectives: [a] the confidentiality of CUI at rest is protected.
whyItMatters: Lost and stolen laptops are the most common CUI incident; encryption turns them into non-events.
evidenceExamples: Screenshot of BitLocker status ('Protection On') on a Windows laptop or FileVault 'On' on a Mac
Screenshot of the MDM/Intune encryption compliance report across all devices
Screenshot of the server's disk encryption or SAN/NAS encryption setting
Screenshot of the cloud storage provider's encryption-at-rest statement for the tenant
Photo of the locked server room if physical protection is claimed for a server that is not encrypted
Screenshot of mobile device encryption status via MDM
aiReviewGuidance: Expect a fleet-wide view (MDM/compliance report) or per-device screenshots for small fleets showing encryption on, plus coverage of servers, phones, and cloud storage. A single laptop screenshot is not fleet evidence. If physical protection is claimed instead of encryption, require the PE evidence and a justification. Reject screenshots showing 'Encryption off', 'Suspended', or devices missing from the compliance report. Note the FIPS requirement from SC.L2-3.13.11.
commonFailures: Encryption enabled on some laptops but not all
Servers and NAS unencrypted and in a shared space
Phones with CUI email not managed or encrypted
Recovery keys not escrowed, so encryption gets turned off after a lockout

title: Monitor Communications for Attacks
officialText: Monitor organizational systems, including inbound and outbound communications traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
plainEnglish: Something (an EDR agent, firewall IDS/IPS, or a managed security service) is watching your network traffic in both directions and your computers for signs of attack, and someone gets the alerts.
assessmentObjectives: [a] the system is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks;
[b] inbound communications traffic is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks; and
[c] outbound communications traffic is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
whyItMatters: Attacks that go unnoticed for months are the ones that cost the most; monitoring shortens that window to hours.
evidenceExamples: Screenshot of the EDR/XDR console (Microsoft Defender for Business, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) showing all devices reporting and alerts enabled
Screenshot of the firewall's IDS/IPS feature enabled with recent events
Screenshot of the firewall log showing outbound connections are logged, or DNS filtering (e.g., Cisco Umbrella) blocking events
Screenshot of the alert-notification settings showing who receives alerts
MSSP/SOC service agreement and a sample monthly report
Short written description of what is monitored, by what tool, and who reviews it
aiReviewGuidance: Look for host monitoring (EDR console) and network monitoring (IDS/IPS or firewall logging) that explicitly covers outbound traffic, which is the usual gap. A firewall screenshot showing only inbound blocking does not satisfy [c]. Alert routing to a named person or SOC is required to count as 'monitoring' rather than 'logging'. Reject if the EDR console shows devices offline for weeks or if IDS/IPS is 'available but disabled'. Assessors will interview whoever reviews alerts.
commonFailures: Logs are collected but nobody is alerted or reviews them
Outbound traffic not monitored at all
IDS/IPS licence expired or feature never turned on
EDR deployed to some but not all devices
